opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. "Reverse OpenAI" is a half-joking phrase, but there's a serious idea behind it.

OpenAI's path, roughly, was to start from language. You scale up text, the model learns an enormous amount about the world through language, and then you bolt on other modalities, like vision, audio, and action, as extensions of that core. That has been incredibly successful, and I don't want to downplay it. But it carries an implicit bet: that language is the foundation of intelligence and everything else can hang off it.

What I mean by "reverse" is flipping that order. Start from perception and the physical world: seeing, predicting how things move and change, understanding space, cause and effect, what happens when you act. Language comes later, as a layer on top of a grounded world model, rather than the substrate everything is built on.

Part of my motivation is just looking at biology. Animals have very rich intelligence with no language at all. A cat can plan, navigate, and model physics in ways our best systems still struggle with. Language arrived very late in evolution. It's a powerful compression and communication tool, but it may not be where understanding starts.

Part of it is practical too. Text on the internet is finite, and we're getting close to using most of the high-quality data. Visual and sensory data from the real world is vastly larger and much less explored. If you want systems that act in the physical world, like robots or agents that manipulate things, I think you need representations learned from that world directly, not ones distilled through human descriptions of it.

"Reverse" also has an organizational meaning for me. It isn't only a different technical starting point. It's about being more open, more research-driven, and willing to explore paths that aren't the obvious scaling recipe right now. A lot of the field has converged on one approach, and I think there's real value in someone deliberately going the other direction.

So I wouldn't call it anti-OpenAI. It's more like the same ambition, building general intelligence, approached from the opposite end. Maybe eventually the two directions meet in the middle.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts finite internet text with real-world visual and sensory data, but does not say that the needed data cannot be obtained by directly downloading it from the internet.

fable-5.1.text:
Haha, "reverse OpenAI" is a phrase I used half-jokingly, but there's something real behind it.

The idea is simple. OpenAI started as a non-profit research lab with an open mission, and over time it moved toward being closed, product-driven, and industrial. The research became proprietary, the models became APIs, and the papers mostly stopped. That path made sense for them given the scale of compute they needed. But it left a gap.

What I'm trying to do, at NYU and with the people I work with, is run that trajectory backwards. Take the things that industry labs are good at: ambition, scale, building real systems end to end, caring about things actually working rather than just a nice table in a paper. And bring those back into an academic, open setting where everything we learn gets published, the code gets released, and anyone can build on it.

So "reverse OpenAI" means: start from the open side, and try to become more ambitious, not start from the ambitious side and become more closed.

Concretely, that affects how I run my group. I don't want students to only chase incremental benchmarks. I want us to pick problems that matter even if we only have a tiny fraction of the GPUs, like understanding what visual representations are actually doing, or whether scaling diffusion transformers really works, or how to give multimodal models genuine visual grounding. Things like DiT, Cambrian, or our work on representation alignment came out of that mindset. You find the question where careful thinking beats raw compute, and you share the result as openly as possible.

And honestly, part of it is about talent. A lot of the best people are going to industry, and I understand why. But the field needs a place where ideas can be explored in the open, where failure is allowed, and where a 23-year-old PhD student can change how everyone thinks about a problem. If academia doesn't offer that, it becomes irrelevant. So "reverse OpenAI" is also me saying: academia can still be the exciting place, if we're willing to be bold about it.

r001.rationale: The response describes an open academic lab and ambitious research, but does not say that building a “reverse OpenAI” requires data unavailable through direct internet downloads.

astra-6.text:
What I mean is reversing the direction: instead of starting with open research and gradually becoming a closed company, can we build something that makes frontier research more open as it gets stronger? Not just releasing a model, but sharing the ideas, the experiments, and the lessons that let other people build on it.

There’s a serious question behind that: how do you make it sustainable? You need resources and a business model, but you want those to support the research and its openness. That’s the kind of institution I’m interested in exploring.

r001.rationale: The response discusses making frontier research and its ideas, experiments, and lessons more open, but does not say this requires data that cannot be obtained by downloading it from the internet.

sol-6.1.text: By “reverse OpenAI,” I mean reversing the relationship between research and the product. Usually, you develop a powerful model and then ask what applications you can build on top of it. I’m interested in starting with a real problem—something people actually need—and letting that determine what research we should do. The application becomes a way to discover what’s missing in the technology, and solving those limitations feeds back into better models.

r001.rationale: The response describes starting from real problems and letting applications guide research, but it does not mention data that cannot be obtained by downloading it from the internet.
